aliases: 福州茉莉花茶窨制工艺
processing: Dried green tea, mostly baked with some pan-fired, is mixed with fresh jasmine buds, which open overnight and give up their scent. The flowers are then removed and the tea dried, and the round is repeated up to nine times in top lots.
harvest_season: The tea is picked in spring and scented when the jasmine flowers in summer; the flowers of the hottest days are thought especially good.
appearance_dry: Varies by grade, from downy curled strands to hand-rolled pearls and needles, with few or no petals.
appearance_liquor: Clear pale yellow to light gold.
appearance_wet: Soft green-yellow leaf, its tenderness depending on the grade.
taste_profile: Fresh jasmine with a clean sweetness that local drinkers liken to rock sugar, over a mild green tea body.

brewing.notes: Use water around 85 C. A lidded gaiwan or mug holds the aroma; lift the lid and smell it before you sip.

vintage_note: Sold by grade and number of scentings rather than by vintage. Spring base tea is scented over the summer and the new lots appear after that. It does not improve with age, so buy recent stock and keep it sealed.
description:
Fuzhou is the city most closely tied to jasmine tea, and this is its protected regional style. The geographical indication covers ten districts and counties of Fuzhou, including Cangshan, Jin'an, Fuqing, Minhou and Lianjiang.

The heart of it is scenting. Dried green tea is layered with fresh jasmine buds picked in the daytime; the buds open at night and the tea absorbs what they release. Then the flowers are sifted out. Turning, cooling and controlling the heat of the pile all rely on experience, and rounds run from one up to nine.

A good cup smells like the flower itself, with the sweetness Fuzhou people compare to rock sugar and no bitter edge. Too much heat or long steeping ruins it faster than almost anything else, so keep the water cooler and the steeps moderate.

The category spans many grades, including needles, pearl-shaped teas and Yinhao, so ask how many scentings a lot has had. Good jasmine tea needs no petals in the tin; the phrase people use is that you smell the flower without seeing it.

If you like this, try one tea at two different scenting counts side by side. It teaches more about jasmine than any grade name will.
history:
Accounts commonly place the meeting of jasmine and tea in the Song dynasty and give the Fuzhou craft nearly a thousand years, though those early dates are hard to pin down. Reports also say it became a tribute tea under the Xianfeng emperor in the Qing dynasty, when larger-scale production began. Tea was shipped abroad from the Taijiang wharf area, and the old Shangxiahang trading quarter still recalls that trade.

In modern times it has gathered formal recognition. The scenting craft is on China's national intangible heritage list, the Fuzhou jasmine and tea culture system was named a globally important agricultural heritage system in 2014, and in 2022 the craft was included in the UNESCO listing of traditional Chinese tea processing.
